name: Gilgamesh: A New English Version
date: Free Press (Simon & Schuster), New York, 2004 (hardcover ISBN 9780743261647; paperback 2006, ISBN 9780743261692). UK edition Profile Books, 2005. Held in over 2,700 WorldCat libraries.
creator: Stephen Mitchell (born 1943, Brooklyn), American poet and translator of sacred and classic texts (Tao Te Ching 1988, Book of Job, Bhagavad Gita, later the Iliad and Odyssey), who describes himself as 'de-educated through intensive Zen practice'. Married to the self-help writer Byron Katie, whom he quotes in the Gilgamesh introduction.
form: Free verse adaptation, explicitly called a 'version' and not a translation. The poem is divided into eleven 'Books' (Prologue plus Books I to XI) rather than tablets, preceded by a roughly 60-page interpretive introduction ('The Oldest Story in the World') and followed by about 100 pages of notes, a bibliography and a glossary. Paperback runs about 290 pages.
translator_access: Mitchell has no Akkadian. From 'About This Version': 'I don't read cuneiform and have no knowledge of Akkadian; for the meaning of the text, I have depended on literal translations by seven scholars.' His method was to read and compare the translations in his bibliography, 'cobbled together a rough prose version', and then begin 'the real work, of raising the language to the level of English verse'. He likens the first stage to being 'rather like a bat, feeling out the contours of the original text by flinging sound waves into the dark.' The cribs he names: A. R. George's two-volume critical edition (2003), which he calls 'superb, meticulous, monumental', plus the translations of Jean Bottéro, Benjamin R. Foster, Maureen Gallery Kovacs, Albert Schott, and Raymond Jacques Tournay with Aaron Shaffer. He also read the literary versions of David Ferry and Raoul Schrott. Bottéro's notes shaped his reading of many passages.
scholarly_adviser: None named. Unlike Armitage (Jacob Dahl) or Ferry (William Moran), Mitchell had no personal Assyriologist collaborator. He relied on published scholarship, above all Andrew George's The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic (2003) and Jean Bottéro's French translation and notes. [uncertain: acknowledgments page not checked for private consultations]
versions_used: Base text is Sin-leqi-unninni's Standard Babylonian version ('a sometimes free, sometimes close adaptation into English verse of Sin-leqi-unninni's Standard Version'). Gaps are filled from the Old Babylonian version (for example Shiduri's speech on enjoying life in Book X) and, going further than scholarly translators, from the Sumerian Gilgamesh poems: 'occasionally, when the Standard Version is particularly fragmentary, I have supplemented it with passages from the Sumerian Gilgamesh poems' (e.g. 'Gilgamesh and Huwawa'). Middle Babylonian material is used too (e.g. 'may wild dogs camp in your bedroom' in Enkidu's curse is drawn from the Ur tablet, per the notes). The Schøyen tablets are cited in the notes. Nothing later than George 2003, so no Sulaymaniyah tablet (published 2014).
non_standard_material: Silent merge on the page, documented in the endnotes. The verse carries no brackets, italics or other signals separating Standard Babylonian from Old Babylonian, Sumerian or Mitchell's own additions. Mitchell says so directly: 'I filled in the many gaps in the text; I changed images that were unclear; I added lines when the drama of the situation called for elaboration or when passages ended abruptly and needed transitions; I cut out a number of fragmentary passages; and when the text was garbled, I occasionally changed the order of passages. (All these changes are documented in the notes.)' The notes, keyed by page and phrase, often give George's or Bottéro's literal wording for comparison.
gap_policy: Bridged and smoothed. Mitchell fills lacunae with invented or imported lines, cuts fragments he cannot use, and removes the formulaic repetitions and counting sequences ('the word-for-word repetitions of entire passages and the enumerations from one to seven or twelve'), which he calls 'tedious for us'. Danny Yee's comparative review says he 'fills in the gaps and removes repetitions and stylistic awkwardnesses' while taking 'fewer liberties' than Mason or Ferry, and gives a damaged Tablet V line as an example of a 'simple, straightforward' reading with no marker of loss.
typography_of_absence: Nothing on the page. No square brackets, ellipses, blank lines or line numbers in the poem. The only trace of damage is in the endnotes, where Mitchell sometimes reproduces George's bracketed restorations (e.g. '[like a crack in the ground.]') to show what the literal text looks like.
tablet_xii: Dropped from the poem: 'Like many other translators, I have omitted Tablet XII, which most scholars consider as not belonging to the epic.' It is discussed in the introduction and quoted in the notes (in George's translation, alongside the Sumerian 'Bilgames and the Netherworld'). The effect is a clean ring structure: the book ends on Gilgamesh showing Urshanabi the walls of Uruk, repeating the Prologue, so the last word is the city ('the houses, the public squares') and not Enkidu's report from the underworld.
turning_point: Two hinges. The first, and the one Mitchell's introduction stresses most, is the killing of Humbaba. He reads the Cedar Forest expedition as a moral error: 'Gilgamesh's action is the original preemptive attack', and 'Enkidu caused his own death by insisting that Gilgamesh kill Humbaba; if they had let the monster live, all would have been well.' Humbaba is framed as the forest's guardian appointed by Enlil (a refrain in Book III: 'Humbaba is the forest's guardian'), and after his killing Mitchell doubles the line 'A gentle rain fell onto the mountains.' Enkidu's death follows from this, and Gilgamesh's Book VIII lament ('one of the most beautiful elegies in literature') begins the flight from death. The second hinge is the return to the walls of Uruk. Mitchell argues that the quest itself changes nothing ('The quest proves the futility of the quest'); the advice of Shiduri and Utnapishtim is 'beautiful words, but as useless to him'. The turn comes when Gilgamesh gives up: 'Not until Gilgamesh gives up on transcendence can he realize how beautiful his city is.' The loss of the plant to the snake is the release that makes that surrender possible.
arc_interpretation: Maturity and spiritual growth, read through a Zen and self-inquiry lens. Mitchell's thesis in the introduction: the epic is 'the story of how a man becomes civilized, how he learns to rule himself and therefore his people, and to act with temperance, wisdom, and piety. The poem begins with the city and ends with it.' The arc runs from tyrant to wise king, with failure recast as the path to wisdom: 'Somehow, in the interval between story and return, Gilgamesh has become wise. He has absorbed not the conventional wisdom of a Shiduri or an Utnapishtim, but the deeper wisdom of the poem's narrative voice, a wisdom that is impartial, humorous, civilized, sexual, irreverent, skeptical of moral absolutes.' He reads the quest allegorically as 'the mind's search for control, order, and meaning in a world where everything is constantly disintegrating', quotes Byron Katie ('When I argue with reality, I lose, but only 100 percent of the time') and the Zen master Seng-ts'an ('The struggle between good and evil / is the primal disease of the mind'), and ends: 'When the mind gives up on its quest for control, order, and meaning, it finds that it has come home.' His rendering of the Prologue builds this in: Gilgamesh returns 'exhausted but whole' (George has 'weary but at peace'). This is the strongest growth reading among the major English versions and the one most often charged with importing modern spirituality. Jasper Griffin (NYRB, 2006) pushed back on the upbeat framing, closing: 'An older wisdom, and a truer poetry, sees that the highest nobility and the deepest truth are inseparable, in the end, from failure.' [uncertain: whether Griffin's closing line is aimed at Mitchell's reading specifically]
key_passages: Shamhat and Enkidu (Book I): the most explicit English version. 'She stripped off her robe and lay there naked, / with her legs apart, touching herself. / Enkidu saw her and warily approached. / He sniffed the air. He gazed at her body. / He drew close, Shamhat touched him on the thigh, / touched his penis, and put him inside her. / She used her love-arts, she took his breath / with her kisses, held nothing back, and showed him / what a woman is.' Nicolas Liney (LARB, 3 May 2026) cites this as Mitchell overplaying the scene, 'inserting caresses and body parts'. Shamhat's description of Gilgamesh renders kuzbu as 'how his body pulses with erotic power', which Liney says 'gets closer' than Armitage's 'the very embodiment of manliness and vigor'. Siduri/Shiduri's advice (Book X), from the Old Babylonian text, unmarked: 'Humans are born, they live, then they die, / this is the order that the gods have decreed. / But until the end comes, enjoy your life, / spend it in happiness, not despair. / Savor your food, make each of your days / a delight, bathe and anoint yourself, / wear bright clothes that are sparkling clean, / let music and dancing fill your house, / love the child who holds you by the hand, / and give your wife pleasure in your embrace.' Mitchell's introduction calls it 'a charming piece of conventional wisdom that can do him no earthly good'. Death in the bedchamber (Book XI): 'Gilgamesh cried out, "What shall I do, / where shall I go now? Death has caught me, / it lurks in my bedroom, and everywhere I look, / everywhere I turn, there is only death."' Walls of Uruk (end of Book XI): the Prologue's tour repeated as Gilgamesh's speech to Urshanabi, in five-beat lines, ending 'observe the land it encloses: the palm trees, the gardens, / the orchards, the glorious palaces and temples, the shops / and marketplaces, the houses, the public squares.' Mitchell expands the list of what the wall encloses into a picture of civic life. [uncertain: the full list of expansions against the Akkadian was not checked line by line] Humbaba's death (Book V): gory ('sliced him open, pulled out his intestines, / cut off his head with its knife-sharp teeth') and followed by the repeated 'A gentle rain fell onto the mountains.'
diction_and_metre: Loose four-beat line: 'a loose, noniambic, nonalliterative tetrameter', modelled, he says, on parts of Eliot's Four Quartets and Elizabeth Bishop's 'Sestina'. He varied it 'so that no two consecutive lines have the identical rhythm'. The Prologue and the end of Book XI move to five beats. Diction is plain contemporary American English, occasionally colloquial and blunt, with no archaism. Repetition and numerical formulae are cut, which speeds the narrative. Jasper Griffin: 'lines with four rhythmic stresses, unrhyming, in a diction raised a little in tone, but not unrecognizably far, from that of speech'. Armitage called it 'very fluid and flowing'.
sample_line: "Death has caught me, / it lurks in my bedroom, and everywhere I look, / everywhere I turn, there is only death." (Mitchell, Gilgamesh, Book XI, Free Press 2004)
critical_response: A commercial and classroom success and the most widely read English Gilgamesh of the 2000s, but with a split verdict. Jasper Griffin, 'The True Epic Vision', New York Review of Books, 9 March 2006, called it 'ingenious and very readable' and said Mitchell 'has produced a satisfying result', while noting he 'makes no claim to be a scholar' and relies 'on the work of professionals'. Other reviews: Hudson Review 58.2 (Summer 2005), pp. 329-334; Gay & Lesbian Review Worldwide 12.2 (2005), pp. 38-39. Publishers Weekly praised language 'as swift and strong as the story itself'. Danny Yee's comparison of Mason, Ferry, Mitchell, Dalley and George recommends Mitchell 'for those who want a complete work' and 'a simple, straightforward and "well-marked trail" to the story', capturing 'its structure as well as its emotional power'. In 2026 it became the standard point of comparison for Armitage's version: Armitage told the Pittsburgh Review of Books that Mitchell's was 'the first I read front to back, very fluid and flowing', and Nicolas Liney's LARB review ('The Epic of the Fear of Death', 3 May 2026) uses Mitchell twice, once as closer on kuzbu and once as overplaying the Shamhat scene. Critics from the scholarly side place it among versions by writers 'who seek to make the text glow but who know little about the sources', and blogs and readers repeatedly call it 'too updated'. [uncertain: Hudson Review and Gay & Lesbian Review verdicts not read]
controversies: Three recurring charges. (1) Liberty: a self-declared version by a poet without Akkadian that fills gaps, reorders passages, imports Sumerian material and deletes repetition, with all of this visible only in the notes. (2) Topical politics: the introduction opens 'In Iraq, when the dust blows, stopping men and tanks' and reads the Humbaba expedition 'in eerie counterpoint to the recent American invasion of Iraq', calling it 'the original preemptive attack'; the publisher's copy repeats the line that 'a preemptive attack on a monster can have dire consequences'. Reviewers and later summaries (e.g. Wikipedia's Epic of Gilgamesh article) describe it as a 'controversial translation that takes many liberties with the text and includes modernized allusions and commentary relating to the Iraq war of 2003'. (3) Interpretive imposition: the Zen and Byron Katie framing of the ending, the sympathetic Humbaba, and a sexually explicit Shamhat scene that goes beyond the Akkadian (Liney, LARB 2026). No provenance or authorship dispute. [uncertain: a specific published attack by Andrew George on Mitchell was not found; the George result file in this set also marks this uncertain]
regional_reception: Reception is overwhelmingly Anglophone (US and UK via Profile Books). Its Iraq-war framing addresses an American readership about Iraq, not Iraqi readers. No evidence found of Arabic or Kurdish translation or of reception in Iraq. [uncertain]
ai_craft_tension: Mitchell's own account of his workflow reads like a human version of a modern machine pipeline. Step one: ingest seven scholarly translations and George's edition, compare them, and produce 'a rough prose version'. That is close to what a model can now do in seconds from a transliteration or a stack of cribs. Step two, which he calls 'the real work', is 'raising the language to the level of English verse': choosing a rhythm, deciding which repetitions to cut, where drama needs an added line, and what the whole poem means. His confessed image for the first stage ('rather like a bat, feeling out the contours of the original text by flinging sound waves into the dark') captures working at one remove from the source, which is what an LLM does too. Mitchell also shows the cost. The fluent result erases every gap, merges three recensions and a set of Sumerian poems without a seam, and carries a strong interpretive thesis (Zen surrender, anti-war Humbaba) into the text itself. That is the machine-output worry, but with a human signature: fluency that hides where the source is missing, and a confident voice that reads its own values into the material. The difference is accountability. Mitchell documents every change in 100 pages of notes and signs the introduction that argues his reading. A useful contrast for Lee: the craft is not the crib, it is the choices, and the obligation is to show them.
essay_hooks: 1) The admission: 'I don't read cuneiform and have no knowledge of Akkadian; for the meaning of the text, I have depended on literal translations by seven scholars' (About This Version). 2) The bat: 'I felt rather like a bat, feeling out the contours of the original text by flinging sound waves into the dark.' A human description of working from other people's outputs. 3) Two-stage pipeline: 'cobbled together a rough prose version' then 'the real work, of raising the language to the level of English verse'. 4) The full list of liberties in one sentence: 'I filled in the many gaps in the text; I changed images that were unclear; I added lines when the drama of the situation called for elaboration... I cut out a number of fragmentary passages; and when the text was garbled, I occasionally changed the order of passages.' 5) Opening of the introduction: 'In Iraq, when the dust blows, stopping men and tanks...' and Humbaba as 'the original preemptive attack'. 6) Growth reading in one line: 'Not until Gilgamesh gives up on transcendence can he realize how beautiful his city is.' 7) The 2026 bridge: Armitage said Mitchell's was 'the first I read front to back, very fluid and flowing' (Pittsburgh Review of Books), and LARB's Nicolas Liney set their Shamhat scenes side by side: Mitchell's 'touched his penis, and put him inside her' versus Armitage's 'more blushing and restrained' language. 8) Numbers: 'slightly fewer than two thousand of the three thousand lines' survive in readable form (Mitchell's introduction), against a version that reads as complete.
